judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Plain and short, and the payoff line is Nox-like, but it switches from a posted proclamation ('Attention! By order of...') into a first-person complaint ('my finest diggers'). The 'As if X were not horror enough!' aside repeats a pattern seen elsewhere in the new texts.

items.label: B
items.critique: A frog trapped in a burning house, a '?!', and the player 'saying' he wants loads and loads of money: the dry, slightly absurd humour is Westwood's own.

items.label: C
items.critique: One sentence runs on through four 'and' clauses, far longer than any Nox line. It hands over a quiver with no reason given, and the plot (the mayor can't spare a man because of the Ogres) is spelled out too neatly.

items.label: D
items.critique: The quest comes up casually out of shop talk ('Actually, business has been somewhat slow'), gives a vague goal, and closes with a 'Well done, lad!' / 'young sir' thanks that is typical of Westwood's townsfolk.

items.label: E
items.critique: Opens with 'Good!' in reply to something said earlier, ties the reward to a story item (the petition) and gives a coloured key. The journal entry capitalises Urchin, as Westwood does.

items.label: F
items.critique: Clipped exclamations ('Ruined! Half the winter's meat, ruined!') are built for punch, and 'lock the door behind you' and 'he's got bigger troubles than wolves' feel like a writer's flourishes. The handoff to the next quest-giver reads like a design template.

items.label: G
items.critique: The drawn-out 'Ooooh', the urgent and slightly stiff phrasing ('That evil one defeated both of my novices') and a reward that is really a plot item are all main-quest Westwood.

items.label: H
items.critique: Too many sensory and comic touches piled up ('stung all over', 'lenses are filthy', 'Listen! Not a single...'), plus a setting-bridging complaint about the soldiers, make it a written-up comic vignette rather than Nox's plain quest talk.

items.label: I
items.critique: 'So here's my bargain... Agreed?' and the closing joke 'Now maybe I can finally get some reading done' are modern sitcom timing. The 'As if [Person] and his Undead weren't enough!' aside works the same way as in A and C.

items.label: J
items.critique: Old-fashioned overstatement ('worse than the pox!'), a reward of a title and free passage, and 'I insist' all suit Westwood's town officials. The stiff, odd 'charm and banish' journal entry fits the class-masked original.

tells: The new texts pack the offer with extra colour (sensory detail, comic complaints, why the local authorities won't help). Westwood's offers state the problem, the place and the ask in a few plain sentences.
Run-on or rhythm-built sentences (chains of 'and' clauses, triplets of clipped exclamations) point to the new writing. Westwood's sentences are mostly short and evenly paced.

Sitcom-style closing jokes and bargain framing ('So here's my bargain... Agreed?', 'Deal?', 'Now maybe I can finally...') read modern. Westwood's humour comes from absurd situations and dry, deadpan replies to the player.

The same aside ('As if X weren't enough!') and the same reward ('100 gold pieces') turn up across several texts, which suggests one template. Westwood's quests vary more and often give story items (petitions, titles, keys) as rewards.
Westwood's offers often grow out of a running conversation ('Actually...', 'Good!') rather than opening cold with an exclamation about the pest.
